title: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Simple 2D cellular automata can grow near-perfect circles

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Some simple two-dimensional cellular automata on a square grid grow patterns whose overall shape closely approximates a perfect circle, despite the grid's square symmetry.

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: it is even possible to find cellular automata that yield overall shapes that closely approximate perfect circles.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci A New Kind of Science claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: Stephen Wolfram, A New Kind of Science (Champaign, IL: Wolfram Media, 2002), Chapter 5, “Two Dimensions and Beyond”; section “Cellular Automata” (from p. 170), p. 176. Scope: two-dimensional outer totalistic cellular automata with 8 neighbors

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on wolfram2002-ch05-03: resolvable-now, resolvability 0.91

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A claimed example can be reproduced exactly and its geometry quantified with standard image and lattice methods. Since the core assertion is existential, a robust rule suffices even if asymptotic perfection is not claimed.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run candidate eight-neighbor outer-totalistic rules from one seed and measure radial boundary error, anisotropy, and error scaling relative to the best-fit circle as time increases. A simple rule with small, decreasing relative error and weak fourfold anisotropy confirms the existential claim.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Closely approximates needs a numerical tolerance.

Asymptotic circularity is stronger than finite visual circularity.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
data existence: 0.9
operationalizability: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.95
analysis feasibility: 0.92

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The rule, the initial row, and the claimed circular outline are concrete, and the evolution is an exact finite cellular automaton. Public simulators can run it for far more than the 400 steps in the figure and report a circularity statistic with an obvious confirming or refuting range. Grid anisotropy is precisely what the measurement is designed to detect, so the test discriminates the claim from a merely blob-like growth.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Run the stated eight-neighbor rule (black only with exactly three black neighbors, with the published survival and death cases) from a short row of black cells, and measure circularity and the quadrupolar Fourier component of the boundary against a circle of radius about 0.37t. Circularity staying near 1 at large t confirms the approximation; a persistent square or diamond anisotropy would refute it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
On a square lattice a perfect circle is impossible, so 'closely approximate' needs a numeric tolerance such as circularity or radial error.

Very large t is cheap but not infinite; a late drift away from circularity would still count against the claim.

fields.label: Dimension scores
fields.value:
operationalizability: 0.9
discriminating power: 0.85
data existence: 0.9
analysis feasibility: 0.9
data adequacy: 0.9

fields.label: Hypothesis
fields.value: The two-dimensional 8-neighbour outer totalistic cellular automaton with code 746 (the example Wolfram gives on p. 178), started from a row of 7 black cells, grows a pattern whose outer boundary stays close to a circle: the radial profile of the boundary has small relative spread and no appreciable fourfold (square-lattice) anisotropy, at the 400 steps shown in the book and at three times that many steps.

fields.label: Method
fields.value: analysis.py evolves Wolfram's 8-neighbour outer totalistic code 746 from a row of 7 black cells on a 500x500 (T = 400) and 1100x1100 (T = 1200) grid with numpy, asserting that the pattern never reaches the grid edge. All black cells are binned by polar angle about the centroid into 360 one-degree bins and the largest radius per bin forms the outer profile r(theta); CV = std/mean of that profile and A = mean radius within 5 degrees of the lattice axes over the mean radius within 5 degrees of the diagonals. A control rule in which any black neighbour makes a cell black (which grows a square) was run with the same initial condition to validate that the statistics detect lattice anisotropy.

fields.label: Pass criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. Run code 746 (a white cell becomes black iff exactly 3 of its 8 neighbours are black; a black cell stays black iff it has 0-4 black neighbours and becomes white with 5 or more; Wolfram's outer-totalistic numbering, bit index 2*s + c) from a horizontal row of 7 black cells for T = 400 and T = 1200 steps on a grid large enough that the pattern never touches the edge. Take the centroid of all black cells as centre, bin all black cells by polar angle into 360 one-degree bins and let r(theta) be the largest centre distance in each bin (outer boundary profile). Compute CV = std(r)/mean(r) and the anisotropy ratio A = mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four axis directions divided by the mean of r within +/-5 degrees of the four diagonal directions (a square gives A = 0.707, a diamond 1.414, a circle 1). 'supports' if at T = 1200 both CV <= 0.03 and |A - 1| <= 0.03, and at T = 400 both CV <= 0.05 and |A - 1| <= 0.05. Measurement validation (not part of the verdict): the same statistics for the control rule 'a cell becomes black if any of its 8 neighbours is black' (which grows a square) must give A < 0.8 and CV > 0.06, otherwise the method is declared broken and the verdict is 'inconclusive' with reason 'other'.

fields.label: Fail criterion
fields.value: Pre-registered. 'refutes' if at T = 1200 CV >= 0.06 or |A - 1| >= 0.06 (the outline is at least as far from a circle as a regular octagon is from its circumscribed circle in CV terms, or shows a clear square or diamond bias). Any intermediate outcome -> 'mixed'. Growth rate: the mean radius divided by T is reported and compared with Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t', but does not enter the verdict.

fields.label: Unit
fields.value: CV = std/mean of the 360-bin outer radial profile; A = axis/diagonal mean radius (circle = 1, square = 0.707)

fields.label: Uncertainty
fields.value: deterministic computation; lattice discreteness contributes about 0.5/mean_r = 0.001 to CV at T = 1200

fields.label: Interpretation
fields.value: 'Overall shape' is taken as the outer boundary of the set of black cells (interior holes ignored), and 'closely approximates a perfect circle' as a boundary whose radius varies by at most a few percent around the pattern and shows no lattice-axis bias. The claim is existential ('it is even possible to find cellular automata that ...'), so one rule suffices; the rule tested is the one Wolfram himself exhibits (code 746, p. 178, with the stated initial condition and the 400-step figure). The 1200-step run checks that the circularity is not an artefact of the particular time shown. The pattern is generated by analysis.py; there is no external download.

fields.label: Datasets
fields.value: Two-dimensional 8-neighbour (Moore) outer totalistic cellular automaton, Wolfram code 746, generated by analysis.py; initial condition a row of 7 black cells on a white background; T = 400 and 1200 steps; grid 1100 x 1100 with the pattern kept away from the edges; control rule (code with all 'any black neighbour -> black' bits set) run with the same initial condition and T

fields.label: Caveats
fields.value:
Both pre-registered thresholds were met with margin: at T = 1200 the boundary radius varies by 1.2 % (CV) around the pattern and the axis/diagonal ratio is 1.014; both statistics improved between T = 400 and T = 1200, so the circularity is not a transient of the time shown in the book. The control square gave CV = 0.108 and A = 0.736 (ideal square: 0.707), so the statistics do detect lattice anisotropy.

The measured growth rate is 0.36 cells per step, close to Wolfram's 'about 0.37 t'.

The claim is existential and only the rule Wolfram himself exhibits was tested; nothing is said here about how common circle-growing rules are. A small residual fourfold anisotropy (A = 1.014, slightly diamond-leaning) persists and is not zero, so 'closely approximates' rather than 'is' a circle is the supported reading; whether A tends to 1 as T grows further was not tested beyond 1200 steps.

The outer boundary profile ignores interior holes and surface roughness below the one-degree binning scale.
